newsitem.title: USA: Parental leave an option for fathers, too.
newsitem.headline: Parental leave an option for fathers, too.

text.p: Rebecca's birth on Jan. 4, 1996, brought more than joy into the Nathanson household. It brought her father, Howard, home full-time from his office to care for her.

When his wife Jill returned to her job as vice president at a New York investment banking house 12 weeks after her daughter's birth, Howard took a nine-month parental leave from his duties as programmer/analyst for AT&T Corp. in Basking Ridge, N.J.
He did not draw a salary during this period but his medical coverage was continued and the company guaranteed his return to work at his old job or one comparable to it.
"It was just a decision between do I stay home, do we bring her to day care initially, or do we hire a nanny. I feel I made the right choice," Nathanson said.

"I never had a problem (with self-image), and since my wife is more the breadwinner in the family from an economic standpoint it made more sense, but it was always something I was looking forward to," he explained.
"Generally speaking," said AT&T spokesman Burke Stinson, "the men who are taking advantage of parental leave seem to be the most secure with their brainpower and value to the company.

"My personal view," he added, "is that many men give lip-service to their desire to be better dads, and when it is presented to them, they pass the opportunity by. Men have been getting away with being weekend daddies for a long time."

When AT&T instituted the newborn leave policy back in 1979, only one father participated for every 400 women. That figure is now one for every 18, in part because it is better publicised and also because the name of the plan has been changed from "maternal" or "paternal" leave to the generic "parental" leave, Stinson said.
"I really enjoyed the experience," Nathanson said. "It was wonderful to take care of her day to day, to see her develop as she grew older. I did not really miss going into the office.
"Even for a little more than a month when I was home," he recalled, "I was still getting calls from the office, so I was interacting, but I didn't miss it at all since I had my daughter there.

"What's important in life changes," Nathanson said, "and right now my daughter is more important than my job. There were a few people (co-workers) who were envious because it got me out of the day to day grind of the office."
Father and daughter "spent a lot of time at the mall, where I could walk her around indoors and some days I'd go visit a friend or two," Nathanson said.

"During the summer we would take walks outside, and I would take her to the park. She came with me on whatever errands I had to do, whether to the supermarket or to the store. I was happier being at home. I definitely miss those days."

Social psychologists say that Nathanson's enjoyment of the experience is not unusual. "Men who overcome (the) barriers to take primary care of their children usually value the experience highly," writes Deborah Lee in the just published "Having It All, Having Enough"(Amacom).
Nathanson said because computer work changes so rapidly he felt that if he did not return to work his skills would become obsolete.

"When I was home with her (Rebecca) full-time there were a few things I tried to do, learn new software, etc., and I found that I did not have the time to do that, and that was the reason I decided I had to come back to work now," he said.
Looking back, Nathanson said, "We thought that the first year was very important to get our daughter on a good start. We felt this was a good situation, not only for me but for her."
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
